issues.legal_issue: A transferee who proves derivative title to rented premises succeeds to the original landlord’s tenancy, unless the tenant has attorned to the transferee.
material_facts: The tenant admitted that the former owner owned the premises and had inducted him as a tenant.
The landlord proved the successive transfers of the premises and a partition under which the premises came to her.
The tenant denied the transferee’s title but produced no evidence to rebut the proved transfers.
issues.conclusion: The transferee proved title and became the tenant’s landlord by operation of law, on the same terms as the original tenancy.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 116 of the Evidence Act, 1872, a tenant cannot deny the title of the landlord during the tenancy, but may challenge the derivative title of an assignee or purchaser unless the tenant has attorned to that transferee. Once the transferee proves title, the original tenancy devolves by operation of law on the same terms, unless modified or lawfully determined. The Court relied on Sarkar’s Law of Evidence, 16th Edition, pages 2106–2108, and cited no earlier case.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brings a proceeding under rent-control law to evict a tenant from rented premises.
predicates.original_tenancy_admitted: The tenant admits that the former owner owned the premises and created the tenancy.
predicates.derivative_title_proved: The transferee proves the chain by which title to the premises passed to them.

issues.definition: When a rent-control eviction proceeding involves an admitted original tenancy and proven derivative title, the transferee becomes the landlord under that tenancy.

issues.legal_issue: A second appeal involving a substantial question of law should not be dismissed in limine without identifying the facts, issues, submissions, and applicable legal principles.
material_facts: The High Court dismissed the second appeal in limine, treating the lower courts’ findings as concurrent findings of fact.
The High Court did not set out the facts or the legal principle applicable to the dispute.
The Supreme Court held that the second appeal involved substantial questions of law.
issues.conclusion: The second appeal deserved admission for final hearing, and its cursory dismissal could not be countenanced.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, governs second appeals involving substantial questions of law. The High Court’s cursory disposal without addressing the facts, submissions, points arising, or applicable legal principles was not acceptable. The Court cited no earlier case.

predicates.second_appeal_proceeding: A party brings a second appeal from the decision of the first appellate court.
predicates.substantial_question_of_law_arises: The issues raised in the second appeal include a substantial question of law.
predicates.appeal_dismissed_without_reasoned_consid: The court dismisses the second appeal without setting out and considering the material facts, issues, and applicable legal principles.

issues.definition: A second appeal raising a substantial question of law requires admission for final hearing when it has been dismissed without reasoned consideration.

issues.legal_issue: When findings on the landlord-tenant relationship are reversed and findings on eviction grounds were influenced by those findings, the eviction grounds must be reconsidered by the trial court.
material_facts: The trial court dismissed the eviction suit after finding that the landlord had not proved the landlord-tenant relationship.
The Supreme Court reversed that finding and held that the relationship existed.
The trial court had also decided other issues, but those findings were influenced by its decision on the relationship issue.
issues.conclusion: The suit was remanded to the trial court for a fresh decision on the remaining issues concerning the grounds for eviction.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Section 12 of the M.P. Accommodation Control Act, 1961, which sets out grounds for eviction, and held that the remaining issues should be decided afresh because their findings were influenced by the reversed findings on the landlord-tenant relationship. The Court cited no earlier case.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brings a proceeding under rent-control law seeking eviction on statutory grounds.
predicates.landlord_tenant_finding_reversed: An appellate court reverses the lower court’s finding on whether a landlord-tenant relationship exists.
predicates.remaining_eviction_findings_influenced_b: The lower court’s findings on other eviction grounds were influenced by its finding on the landlord-tenant relationship.

issues.definition: When a reversed landlord-tenant finding influenced the lower court’s findings on other eviction grounds, those grounds require a fresh decision by the trial court.

issues.legal_issue: A transferee who succeeds to the original landlord’s tenancy may determine that tenancy by serving a proper quit notice.
material_facts: After establishing title to the premises, the landlord served the tenant a notice terminating the tenancy and demanding arrears of rent.
The Supreme Court held that the tenant had become the landlord’s tenant on the original terms.
issues.conclusion: The landlord properly determined the tenancy by serving the quit notice, which demanded the balance of rent.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the tenancy devolved on the transferee on the original terms and could be determined by the landlord in accordance with law; it found the notice served in this case to be proper. No specific provision or earlier case was cited for this conclusion.

predicates.transferee_title_proved: A transferee proves title to premises that were subject to an existing tenancy.
predicates.tenancy_devolved_to_transferee: The original tenant’s tenancy passes to the transferee on the original terms.
predicates.quit_notice_served_demanding_rent: The transferee serves the tenant a notice terminating the tenancy and demanding rent due.

issues.definition: When title and devolution of the tenancy are established, service of a quit notice demanding rent properly determines the tenancy.
